passed.title: total_* duration accessors truncate to whole units by default
passed.trap: pandas `Timedelta.total_seconds()` returns a float. The Polars `Expr.dt.total_*` methods default to `fractional=False` and return `Int64`, so the partial unit is dropped. A 90-minute duration gives `1` from `Expr.dt.total_hours`, and 59 seconds gives `0` from `Expr.dt.total_minutes`. Pass `fractional=True` to get a `Float64` that keeps the fractional part.
passed.example:
import polars as pl
from datetime import timedelta

df = pl.DataFrame({"d": [timedelta(minutes=90), timedelta(seconds=59)]})
out = df.select(
    hours_int=pl.col("d").dt.total_hours(),
    hours_frac=pl.col("d").dt.total_hours(fractional=True),
    minutes_int=pl.col("d").dt.total_minutes(),
    minutes_frac=pl.col("d").dt.total_minutes(fractional=True),
)
for row in out.to_dicts():
    print(row)
print(out.schema)

passed.title: weekday is ISO: Monday is 1 and Sunday is 7, not 0 to 6
passed.trap: pandas `dayofweek` numbers Monday as 0 and Sunday as 6. `Expr.dt.weekday` returns the ISO weekday instead, with Monday = 1 and Sunday = 7. A ported weekend filter such as `weekday >= 5` silently tags Fridays as weekend days. In Polars, test for weekends with `>= 6`.
passed.output:

(datetime.date(2024, 1, 6), 6, True, True)
(datetime.date(2024, 1, 7), 7, True, True)
(datetime.date(2024, 1, 8), 1, False, False)

passed.title: Pair ISO week with iso_year, not year
passed.trap: `Expr.dt.week` returns the ISO week number, from 1 to 53. Dates in early January can belong to week 52 or 53 of the previous ISO year, and late-December dates can belong to week 1 of the next one. `Expr.dt.year` returns the calendar year, so grouping by (`year`, `week`) mixes days from different weeks into one bucket. Group by `Expr.dt.iso_year` together with `Expr.dt.week` instead.
passed.example:
import polars as pl
from datetime import date

df = pl.DataFrame({"date": [date(2021, 1, 1), date(2021, 1, 4), date(2024, 12, 30)]})
out = df.with_columns(
    year=pl.col("date").dt.year(),
    iso_year=pl.col("date").dt.iso_year(),
    week=pl.col("date").dt.week(),
)
print(out.columns)
for row in out.rows():
    print(row)

passed.title: truncate('7d') is not truncate('1w'): non-weekly buckets start at the Unix epoch
passed.trap: With `Expr.dt.truncate`, weekly buckets (`'1w'`) start on Monday, but all other buckets start on the Unix epoch, 1970-01-01, which was a Thursday. As a result, `truncate('7d')` produces Thursday-aligned buckets, not Monday ones. Use `'1w'` when you want calendar weeks, and remember that multi-day buckets such as `'2d'` are aligned to the epoch, not to your data.
passed.example:
import polars as pl
from datetime import date

df = pl.DataFrame({"d": [date(2024, 1, 10)]})  # a Wednesday
out = df.with_columns(
    by_1w=pl.col("d").dt.truncate("1w"),
    by_7d=pl.col("d").dt.truncate("7d"),
).with_columns(
    by_1w_weekday=pl.col("by_1w").dt.weekday(),
    by_7d_weekday=pl.col("by_7d").dt.weekday(),
)
for row in out.to_dicts():
    print(row)

passed.title: with_time_unit is deprecated and reinterprets rather than converts
passed.trap: `Expr.dt.with_time_unit` has been deprecated since 0.20.5. It does not modify the underlying integers; it only relabels the unit, so an `ns` column relabelled as `us` jumps tens of thousands of years. If you really need to fix a wrongly labelled unit, cast to `Int64` and then cast to the desired `pl.Datetime`/`pl.Duration`. If you want the same instant in another unit, use `Expr.dt.cast_time_unit`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl
from datetime import datetime

df = pl.DataFrame({"ts": [datetime(2001, 1, 1)]}).with_columns(
    pl.col("ts").cast(pl.Datetime("ns"))
)
out = df.select(
    pl.col("ts"),
    relabel=pl.col("ts").cast(pl.Int64).cast(pl.Datetime("us")),
    convert=pl.col("ts").dt.cast_time_unit("us"),
)
print(out.schema)
print(out.select(pl.all().cast(pl.String)).rows())

Schema({'ts': Datetime(time_unit='ns', time_zone=None), 'relabel': Datetime(time_unit='us', time_zone=None), 'convert': Datetime(time_unit='us', time_zone=None)})

passed.title: total_* requires a Duration column, not a Datetime
passed.trap: The `Expr.dt.total_*` methods extract totals from a `Duration` type. Calling them directly on a `Datetime` column raises an error instead of returning time since the epoch. First build a duration, by subtracting two datetimes or with `Expr.diff`; note that `Expr.diff` yields `null` on the first row. Also pass `fractional=True` if partial days matter.

verification.reason: The output shows Int64 truncation (1 hour and 0 minutes) by default and Float64 fractions (1.5 and 0.983) with `fractional=True`, matching the docstrings.
The output shows Friday as 5, Saturday as 6, Sunday as 7 and Monday as 1, and `>= 5` flags Friday as weekend, exactly as claimed.
The output shows 2021-01-01 as ISO week 53 of 2020 and 2024-12-30 as week 1 of 2025, while `year` gives the calendar year, so the (year, week) collision is real.
The docstring says weekly buckets start on Monday and others on the epoch, and the output shows `'7d'` truncating to Thursday 2024-01-04 versus Monday 2024-01-08 for `'1w'`.

The deprecation version, the relabel-not-convert behaviour, the +32971 jump and the Int64 cast workaround all come from the docstring and output, and `cast_time_unit` preserves the instant in the output.
